name: Memtime
tagline: Record local app activity privately and convert selected blocks into timesheet entries

pricing.basis: annual billing, per user per month

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: 1 user license; private automatic activity capture; no numeric project cap published.
tiers.notes: Shortest term is quarterly at an $18/month equivalent; 2-year rate is $12/month.

tiers.name: Connect
tiers.limits: 1 user license; adds integrations; no numeric project cap published.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: 1 user license; priority service and advanced features; no numeric usage cap published.

pricing.billingTerms: quarterly + annual + 2-year; no month-to-month plan; Enterprise custom
pricing.hiddenCosts: The shortest commitment is 3 months, so the displayed quarterly monthly-equivalent still requires paying a quarter at a time.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Memtime, record local app activity privately and convert selected blocks into timesheet entries. The hard boundary is calendar and project integrations, team reporting, sync, and enterprise controls, plus ubiquitous capture, coaching, and team workflow.
coreLoopDIY: Record local app activity and focused sessions privately, convert selected time blocks into timesheet entries, review patterns locally, and export a transparent activity record.
requirements: optional accessibility permission for app-name tracking
whatYouLose: calendar and project integrations, team reporting, sync, and enterprise controls
moatNotes: ubiquitous capture, coaching, and team workflow
ongoingBurden: idle detection, permissions, app metadata, privacy, notifications, sync, reports, integrations, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Memtime because the timer is simple, but people pay for frictionless capture and a history they trust enough to invoice or change habits from. The recurring cost buys idle detection, permissions, app metadata, privacy, notifications, sync, reports, integrations, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Kimai
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source time-tracking application with projects, reports, and exports.

alternatives.name: Clockify Free
alternatives.desc: Five users get timers and a private auto-tracker; reports stop at 31-day windows and CSV export is paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup; install the Windows/macOS/Linux desktop app for automatic activity tracking
facts.dataFormat: Saved time entries, projects and reports live in Clockify's cloud; raw auto-tracker app and website activity stays in a local desktop database and is uploaded only when converted into a time entry
facts.gapVsPaid: Its automatic tracker is a private local activity list that still needs manual conversion into time entries, so it is less seamless than Memtime's retrospective timeline and calendar-style assignment workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: An account is required, and automatic tracking needs the desktop app plus operating-system activity permissions

alternatives.name: ManicTime Free
alternatives.desc: One computer gets automatic app, site and document history, tags and timesheet export; cloud sync is the billable part.

facts.install: Install the native Windows, macOS or Linux desktop package
facts.dataFormat: Activity history, tags and reports stay on the computer in local SQLite databases; the Windows client uses ManicTimeCore.db and ManicTimeReports.db
facts.gapVsPaid: It captures a rich local history, but the free desktop product has less polished project-accounting integration and cross-device workflow than Memtime's purpose-built timesheet conversion.

alternatives.name: Toggl Track Free
alternatives.desc: Fast timers plus a private desktop activity trail you can promote into entries; formal approvals cost extra.

facts.install: Hosted signup; optionally install the Windows/macOS desktop app, browser extension or mobile app
facts.dataFormat: Time entries, projects and reports sync to the Toggl Track cloud account; the private desktop Timeline activity remains on that device unless the user turns it into a time entry
facts.gapVsPaid: Its Timeline can suggest what happened, but turning that evidence into a complete retrospective timesheet is more manual and less continuous than Memtime's memory timeline.
facts.setupBlocker: An account is required, and passive app/site history needs the desktop app and operating-system permissions

rejectedAlternatives.name: ActivityWatch
rejectedAlternatives.desc: It records local activity beautifully, but does not turn selected blocks into project timesheet entries.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Basic plan and a personal desktop tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Memtime in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, and optional OS accessibility APIs; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: record local app activity and focused sessions privately, convert selected time blocks into timesheet entries, review patterns locally, and export a transparent activity record.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create one-click start and stop, manual entries, idle detection, tags, projects, and notes.
Keep any application-name tracking opt-in and never record window contents or keystrokes.
Add Pomodoro-style focus sessions, break reminders, and an optional allowlist blocker.
Provide daily, weekly, project, and category reports with editable corrections.
Export CSV and JSON and make the underlying event log inspectable.
Add automatic local backups and a privacy screen explaining every collected field.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out employee surveillance.
Deliberately leave out payroll and billing automation.
Deliberately leave out cross-device blocking and behavioral coaching services.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
